papers.title: SRGN aggravates cerebral ischemia/reperfusion injury by inducing SLC7A11 depletion and excessive mitophagy-dependent neuronal death
papers.summary: This study investigates how a protein called SRGN worsens brain damage after stroke-like ischemia/reperfusion injury. SRGN appears to deplete SLC7A11, a protein involved in protecting cells from oxidative stress, which leads to excessive mitophagy (the clearance of damaged mitochondria) and ultimately neuronal death. The findings suggest that blocking SRGN or restoring SLC7A11 could be a therapeutic strategy to protect neurons during ischemic brain injury.
papers.why: This paper is directly relevant to the project's focus on mitophagy-dependent neuronal death and its molecular regulation in the brain, offering mechanistic insight that could inform future spatial transcriptomic/metabolomic investigations of mitophagy pathways in diseased neural tissue.
papers.figure: A figure showing the proposed mechanistic pathway linking SRGN, SLC7A11 depletion, and mitophagy induction in neurons.

papers.title: MitoFLUX-EM reveals damaged mitochondria are captured by pre-existing mitolysosomes during PINK1-dependent mitophagy in the heart
papers.summary: This paper introduces MitoFLUX-EM, a new electron microscopy-based method to track mitochondrial turnover in heart tissue. The researchers found that damaged mitochondria are not simply engulfed by newly forming autophagosomes, but are instead captured by already-existing mitolysosomes during PINK1-dependent mitophagy. This challenges the conventional model of sequential autophagosome formation followed by lysosomal fusion, suggesting a more dynamic and opportunistic clearance mechanism.
papers.why: Although this study is in cardiac tissue, it provides a mechanistic and methodological framework for studying mitophagy dynamics via imaging that could directly inform how mitochondrial quality control is investigated in neurons and interneurons.
papers.figure: The figure showing MitoFLUX-EM imaging of damaged mitochondria being captured by pre-existing mitolysosomes, likely depicting the sequential or snapshot EM data supporting this capture mechanism.

papers.title: Mitophagy in pathogenesis and therapeutic implications for infection.
papers.summary: This paper reviews how mitophagy, the selective autophagic clearance of damaged mitochondria, influences the course and outcome of infections by various pathogens. It discusses how pathogens can manipulate mitophagy pathways to evade immune responses or promote their own survival within host cells. The review also considers mitophagy-targeting strategies as potential therapeutic interventions for infectious diseases.
papers.why: Although focused on infection rather than neurons, this review could offer mechanistic insights into mitophagy regulatory pathways that may generalize to understanding mitochondrial quality control in neurons and interneurons.

papers.title: Alphavirus Nsp3 protein hijacks receptor-mediated mitophagy via BNIP3L/NIX to dampen IFN response and promote viral replication.
papers.summary: This paper shows that a protein from alphaviruses, called Nsp3, manipulates a specific form of mitochondrial quality control called receptor-mediated mitophagy. It does this by exploiting the BNIP3L/NIX receptor, which normally helps cells clear damaged mitochondria. By hijacking this pathway, the virus suppresses the host's interferon (antiviral immune) response, allowing it to replicate more efficiently.
papers.why: Although focused on viral infection rather than neurons, this paper offers mechanistic insight into BNIP3L/NIX-mediated mitophagy regulation, a core pathway relevant to understanding mitophagy dysregulation in neurons and interneurons.

papers.title: The WD40 domain of autophagy protein ATG-16.2 is required for lysosomal regulation and longevity in germline-less C. elegans
papers.summary: This paper studies ATG-16.2, a C. elegans autophagy protein, and finds that its WD40 domain is specifically required for proper lysosomal function and for extending lifespan in germline-less worms. Loss of this domain disrupts lysosomal regulation even though other autophagy functions may remain intact, suggesting the WD40 domain has a specialized role beyond core autophagosome formation. The findings link a specific protein domain to the broader connection between autophagy, lysosomal biology, and organismal longevity in a germline-less context.
papers.why: This work on domain-specific regulation of autophagy and lysosomal function by ATG-16.2 offers mechanistic insight that could inform understanding of mitophagy and lysosomal regulation in neurons, even though the model system and tissue context differ substantially from the brain focus of the profile.

papers.title: Needle-knife attenuates excessive autophagy and ferroptosis in post-stroke spastic hemiplegia: Association with SDC1/NRF2/SLC7A11/GPX4 pathway.
papers.summary: This study investigates a traditional Chinese medicine technique called needle-knife therapy in a model of post-stroke spastic hemiplegia, a condition causing muscle stiffness after stroke. The researchers found that needle-knife treatment reduced excessive autophagy (a cell recycling process) and ferroptosis (an iron-dependent form of cell death) in affected tissue. These effects were linked to changes in a specific molecular pathway involving SDC1, NRF2, SLC7A11, and GPX4 proteins.
papers.why: While this paper focuses on a different therapeutic context (muscle/motor pathology after stroke) rather than neuronal mitophagy or interneurons specifically, it offers mechanistic insight into autophagy-ferroptosis crosstalk pathways that could inform understanding of related degenerative processes in brain tissue.

papers.title: Mitochondrial dynamics and repair differences in two mouse models of Friedreich's ataxia.
papers.summary: This study compares mitochondrial dynamics and DNA repair processes in two different mouse models of Friedreich's ataxia, a genetic disease caused by frataxin deficiency that leads to mitochondrial dysfunction. The researchers likely examined differences in mitochondrial fission, fusion, and repair mechanisms between the models to understand disease progression. Such comparisons help clarify how genetic background or model design influences mitochondrial pathology in neurodegenerative conditions.
papers.why: Friedreich's ataxia models provide insight into mitochondrial dysfunction and quality control mechanisms relevant to mitophagy in neurons, which is directly applicable to the PhD project's focus on mitochondrial health in neuronal populations.

papers.title: Rethinking mitochondrial isolation for the next generation of mitochondrial therapies
papers.summary: This paper discusses the challenges and rethinking needed for isolating mitochondria to support emerging mitochondrial-based therapies. It likely covers current methodological limitations in extracting intact, functional mitochondria from cells or tissues. The focus is on improving isolation techniques to enable clinical and research applications of mitochondrial transfer or transplantation therapies.
papers.why: Understanding advances in mitochondrial isolation techniques could inform methodologies for studying mitophagy and mitochondrial quality control in neurons, particularly relevant to interneuron health and function.
